extracted.intended_audience: graduate students (and advanced undergraduates) in theoretical computer science interested in geometric/algorithmic techniques; MIT OCW viewers
extracted.subtask_description: Syllabus for an advanced graduate course covering geometric techniques used in modern algorithm design (spectral graph theory, convex geometry, multiplicative weights, lattices, iterative linear algebra methods, LP/SDP approximations). Specifies goals, prerequisites, assessment components, collaboration policy, and lecture schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course assessment components
rubrics_metrics.description: The course requirements will comprise two parts: Problem sets, and Scribe notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the only stated formal requirements; problem sets will be handed out and corrected, and scribe notes will be collected for lectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem sets requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: I will hand out problem sets for each major topic and correct them, but I will not expect you to do all of the problems that I distribute. I will expect students to do as many as is necessary for a good-faith effort to learn the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: a total equivalent to at least two graduate problem sets over the course of the semester. Undergraduates will have a slightly more concrete specified number of required problems. Instructor intends not to impose an onerous workload but to give enough problems to allow real learning; students are trusted to trade off quantity vs. learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scribe notes expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: I would like to have scribes for every lecture. Each student should do his/her fair share of these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scribe notes are a formal part of the course requirements; students are expected to contribute a fair share across the class so that every lecture is covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration policy for problem sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaboration is encouraged on the problem sets. However, you should think about the problems yourself before discussing them with others. Furthermore, you must write your solutions up individually and understand anything that you hand in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you do collaborate, you must acknowledge your collaborators in your writeup. Use of outside sources is strongly discouraged; if, however, you do use an outside source, you must reference it in your solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites and assumed background
rubrics_metrics.description: This is a graduate-level class and will move fairly quickly. We shall assume a significant level of mathematical maturity. The formal prerequisites are fairly minimal however; they consist of: Multivariable Calculus (18.02), Linear Algebra (18.06), Basic Algorithms, and Basic Probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some experience with algorithms beyond the introductory level will be helpful, but it is not strictly necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course goals / learning outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: To learn a collection of powerful (and interrelated) mathematical techniques for algorithm design; topics are picked to be both mathematically interesting and practically useful; will sometimes have long mathematical interludes, but always with proportional algorithmic payoffs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A key goal is to be able to apply these tools directly to your research (whether theoretical or applied); instructor will suggest open research questions whenever possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course logistics — meeting times and pacing
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The course covers many advanced topics and is ambitious in scope; pacing is intended for graduate students and may be brisk given the twice-weekly lecture schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor stance on workload and student responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructor does not want the course to present an onerous workload but wants to give enough problems to allow people to really learn the material; since this is an advanced graduate class, students are capable of deciding for themselves how best to make this tradeoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor will provide problems and corrections but places responsibility on students to choose an appropriate amount of work to achieve genuine learning (see recommended problem-set equivalence).
